  TFLOP/s, above the ceiling, so the compiler dropped MMAs and that arm is
  not a measurement. *Redo*: each phase removed with its result kept live
  (folded into the stored O), so the MMA-only floor of the transposed loop
  is a real number. If it is ~40, the softmax is not the cost and A1 is
  the whole story; if 45+, A2 is worth up to 15%.

**Int8 and Q4 weights** (the LLM's prefill, Kev, embeddings, video's
dequant pass): **G5** builds the B fragment in registers from the bytes
the lane loads itself, using the element order the probe pins (A: lane l
holds row l%16, element e is column e; B: lane l holds column l%16,
element e is row e). No LDS, no barrier, and the plain path stays as the
fallback the probe selects. The MoE Q4 GEMM's 51% is the first customer;
the LLM's prefill graph runs at 9.8 TFLOP/s of useful work (P11), most of
it on these kernels.

=====
## How to run

- The suite: `go run ./cmd/bench -h`; families `peak`, `gemm_wmma`,
  `shapes`, `stride`, `moe`, `bank`. Results append to `results/*.csv`
  with sclk and power columns; the harness warms the clock to 97% first
  (§0.2).
- The ISA: `RADV_DEBUG=shaderstats go run ./cmd/probe shaders/X.spv [32|64]`
  and `RADV_DEBUG=asm …` (`MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DISABLE=1` for a repeat).
  Builds are `go generate ./shaders` lines in `shaders/shaders.go`; `.spv`
  is gitignored.
- A GEMM build from disk through H3: `H3_GEMM_SPV=path` (`H3_GEMM_WAVE=32`
  to pin the wave, `H3_GEMM_KRANGE_SPV=path` for the split down
  projection's companion), `H3_GEMM_REF=file` the bit-identical gate
  (written by the first run, compared by every later one); a loaded
  build that is wrong by construction (`L0_LOADS`, `STAGE_L0`) is still
  timed. The clock and power beside it: a 100 ms loop over
  `hwmon/freq1_input` and `power1_average` (G7 will fold it into
  `bench/sysmon.go`).
- The vertical screens: VIDEO.md M7/M11c/M11h (`H3_SHAPES=480 H3_PROFILE=1
  H3_BANK=q8`, `H3_ATTN_SPV`, `H3_CHUNK`), the image DiT's ladder in
  `research/stage-4-dit-graph.md`, Kev's `cmd/kevload`, the LLM's
  `cmd/llm -bench` (memory: it needs `LLM_BANK_CACHE`).
- A MoE GEMM build from disk: `LLM_MOE_SPV=up_q4k_m4=path.spv[,…]`
  (`cmd/llm` needs `-model` as the **shard**, not the checkpoint
  directory, which holds four GGUFs and is refused; before trusting a
  pass, load a wrong-by-construction build through the same override
  and see the gate fail)
  (`LLM_MOE_SPV_WAVE=32` for a wave32 build; `LLM_MOE_PAD=64` for a build
  without `-DSHORT`, since §2.12 the schedule aligns to 16 and a plain
  build would write the next expert's rows; the shared expert runs the
  `q80` builds of the same rungs) on `cmd/llm -moe` and on the
  `llm` tests, which run from `llm/`; `cmd/llm -moe -model <shard>
  -tokens 2048 -iters 60` is ~2 s of device time an arm, so the clock is
  the median of the samples above 100 W.
- Never edit a shader during a sweep; build the test binary to the
  scratchpad first, and check `ps` for another device run.
- Driver pinned in the record: Mesa 26.2.2 (RADV), glslc 2026.3, Vulkan
  1.4.354, kernel 7.1.8. A driver upgrade re-runs G0.

One workgroup a token, the output held in ten registers a thread already had spare, is **1.37-1.44x on the kernel** and bit-identical (each stream still reduces through the same 256-way tree), taking the graph to **1191.8 / 1372.2 tok/s** at 2048 / 8192 rows and 64k prefill to **654 tok/s** from 440. research/README.md:117:| [P16](p16-decode-arena-width.md) | **The wide batch never cost decode anything: two moves padded to the arena.** Decode **1.16x at every depth** at ubatch 2048 (29.73 → **34.4 tok/s** at depth zero, 27.20 → **31.5** at 128 000 cells), prefill flat, all three changes exact. **The cost P12-7 and P15 measured for a wide `-llm-batch` was a bug**: `DeltaNetGPU.InPort` and `AttnGPU.InPort` advertised the arena's rows, so every decode step zero-filled the whole prefill arena of both blocks' A operand once a layer — `move` 5.5 → 19.7 µs and the qkv projection behind it 1.9x at an 8192-row arena, found by staging wide arenas and prefilling narrow (`-depth -ubatch`), which showed the cost follows the arena and not the prefill. Padding to `roundUp(rows, rowAlign)` takes an 8192 arena's decode 23.55 → **33.87** (1.44x), and through the server decode is **34.2 tok/s at 2048, 4096 and 8192 alike** (P12-7: 28.04 and 25.81) — the break-even is gone. **`hc.cn` goes back to a stream a workgroup at decode** (25.0 → 7.0 µs, 1.06x of a token): P11's workgroup a token is one workgroup on forty CUs walking four streams in series. **`attn.select`'s emit walks blocks, not cells** (68 → 55 µs at 128k). Two refusals: batching the histogram's loads (0.96x) and folding same-bucket lanes before the atomic (0.69x). |
research/README.md:121:| [P12](p12-prefill-round-two.md) | **Prefill round two: two bit-exact kernel changes, and four of P11's own leads measured away.** Prefill is **1.012-1.025x on both axes** — 1191.2 → **1207.7 tok/s** at 2048 rows, 1370.5 → **1403.9** at 8192 (**3.59x** llama.cpp), and 651.3 → **667.7** at 64 000 cells — with the two base passes agreeing to 1370.5/1370.5 and 651.3/651.2. Two changes hold. **The attention kernel's row max ran on sixteen lanes of sixty-four**: `for (i = lane; i < BM; i += WAVE)` with BM 16 and WAVE 64, KTIL times a block, two barriers and a store around each pass, each active lane then walking TILE cells serially with a `selected()` bit test. The whole key block is now staged at once (`stage` holds QT\*KTIL tiles, 2 KB of LDS) and RCL = WAVE/BM lanes share a row, folded by a **clustered subgroup max** — **bit-identical**, because a max has no rounding and the cells scanned are the same ones in the same order, and the wave is converged where the op is issued. **1.16x on the kernel at 512 tokens** and **+1.6-1.8% of a prefill token from 8000 cells on**. And **a K-quant block's header is one sixteen-byte load, not four dwords**: Q4_K/Q5_K open every block with `d`, `dmin` and twelve packed scale bytes, so at BK 32 a lane was issuing eight scalar loads a K-step against the nibbles' four `uvec4`s — L5b-7's rule for the third time. Every block of both formats is 16-byte aligned (region, row and block all multiples of 16) and `MoEGPU.build` now says so rather than trusting it; with the nibble extracted in two ops instead of four it is **`moe.up` 12 118 → 11 755 µs at 2048 tokens (1.031x)** with **`moe.down` (IQ4_NL, untouched) flat as the control**. **And four refusals, which close most of P11's open list.** **Both of `hc.cn`'s named suspects cost nothing**: deleting the 256-way reduction tree outright measures **5331.5 µs against 5325.8** — the eight barriers four times a token are **free**, so the non-bit-exact rewrite queued behind them would have bought zero — and replacing the per-token `gamma` read with a constant measures **5332.9**, because it is the same 40 KB every token and the MALL serves it. Its 57% of copy bandwidth is now unexplained *and* out of hypotheses. **The block skip hoisted out of the loop is 1.00x at every depth**: at 64k a query tile walks ~2000 blocks and skips ~1480, each paying a **dependent** global read, and a cost model where a dead block is ~20% of a live one reproduces `attn.attn`'s 9.8-against-16.0 TFLOP/s exactly — so the whole key range was voted on up front in one coalesced pass with a subgroup ballot, no atomics and no per-block barrier, and it bought **nothing**. The reason is the **exact converse of P8**: a decode step dispatches 24 single-wave workgroups and nothing hides a serial walk, but a 2048-token prefill dispatches **3072**, so that latency is already covered — *latency that matters at decode does not matter at prefill, because prefill has occupancy*. It is still live for decode, where it was deliberately never built. **The selection mask loop is 3.5-8%**, not the rest of the gap. **The MoE's per-element affine is a floor**: gutting the whole scale path is 1.21x at 2048 tokens, P12-2 takes the loads and integer ops out of that, and what remains — an int→float convert, an FMA and an f16 convert on every weight — has no bit-exact cheaper form, since packed fp16 costs thirteen bits of mantissa and `v_cvt_pkrtz` rounds the wrong way. **The ubatch remains the largest number on the board**: 2048 → 8192 is 1.16x and the curve has not flattened, which is a memory budget rather than a kernel. |
research/README.md:122:| [P11](p11-prefill.md) | **Prompt processing: the ubatch was the largest number in the file and the cheapest, and the MoE's row padding is not a cost at all.** `cmd/serve` prefilled in **512-token chunks** because that is llama.cpp's best ubatch and what every number in this vertical is quoted against — and 512 is the **worst rung this graph has**. llama.cpp plateaus at its ubatch; this one does not, because the MoE's arithmetic intensity is the **routing's**: at 512 tokens 274 of 512 experts are unpacked whole to serve 5120 rows, and the schedule pads those out to 11 904. `-llm-batch` is now **2048** — 1.12 GB of arenas for **1.64x** (667.4 → 1093.3 tok/s at 48 layers and ctx 4096; **667 → 1053 through HTTP** on a 4128-token prompt), where the 1.49 GB to 4096 buys 13% more. Separately, `llm_moe_gemm.comp`'s MODE 0 stages BM **scattered** rows of the block input into LDS per K-step, and it was doing it one half at a time: **32 two-byte loads a lane a K-step at BM 64**, against the eight the B unpack issues for four times the data. That is L5b-7's finding on the *operand* instead of the weight — the kernel is bound by how many load instructions it issues — so the halves arena is bound a second time as `uvec4` (binding 7) and a row is four aligned loads: **`moe.up` 14 918 → 11 936 µs a layer at 2048 tokens (1.25x)**, bit for bit the same slab, MODE 1 untouched as the control. The graph: **1079.6 → 1165.1 tok/s at 2048 rows, 1250.1 → 1328.5 at 8192 (3.40x llama.cpp)**, two runs agreeing to 0.2%. **Three changes that look right and are not**, all reverted, all one answer: a 16-row alignment with a row count per record (13.7 ms against 11.9 — the per-fragment branch inside the unrolled accumulator loops costs more than 35% of the rows, and the kernel goes to 256 VGPRs), three sub-lists one dispatch a rung (12.5 — no guard anywhere, but small grids do not fill the machine and three grids have three ramps), and a **128-row block** (13.5 — 608 tiles to 477 but the padding to 2.98x, because with 399 experts touched **the floor is one tile an expert** however wide the block). **At prefill this GEMM is bound by its per-tile slab unpack and the rows are very nearly free**; L5b built the padding as a cost to justify and it is not one, so the way in is fewer *tiles*, which is a bigger ubatch — which is the result. **A second round takes it to 3.51x.** `hc.cn` — the combine fused with the next mixer's norm, the second largest kernel in a prefill and one that does **no arithmetic** — was one workgroup per (token, stream), and the four streams of a token combine *the same* block output row: 110 KB a token where 80 would do. One workgroup a token, the output held in ten registers a thread already had spare, is **1.37-1.44x on the kernel** and bit-identical (each stream still reduces through the same 256-way tree), taking the graph to **1191.8 / 1372.2 tok/s** at 2048 / 8192 rows and 64k prefill to **654 tok/s** from 440. And `AttnGPU.SelSkip` measures, for the first time, **how much of the key axis the QSA selection actually lets the attention kernel skip**: at 64 000 cells the shipped 16x32 tile keeps **25.9%** of (query tile, key block) pairs live, a 16-cell tile would keep 18.5%, and a single query row 14.7% — so **a per-query gather is worth 1.76x, not the 31x the 3.2% density suggests**, which is L4b's "at prefill the density makes it pointless" with a number on it. The 1.40x between a 32-cell block and a 16-cell one was built as a bit-identical per-k-tile skip and is **1.18x slower** (866.1 → 737.2 tok/s at 16k), and at 64k slow enough to hold the ring past P0's two-second watchdog. Two kernels, one rule: **a branch inside an unrolled cooperative-matrix loop costs more than the work it removes** — neither kernel is arithmetic-bound, so change the loop's granularity, not what happens inside it. What is left of the depth term is that `attn.attn` does its useful work at **9.8 TFLOP/s at 64k against 16.0 at depth zero**, and the row max it only runs when the selection is on uses **sixteen of sixty-four lanes** |

content.content:
---
name: h3-gemm-screen-recipe
description: "How to screen a dit_gemm.comp build on H3's real shapes with clocks and a bit-identical gate (H3_GEMM_SPV/WAVE/KRANGE_SPV/REF), ~2.5 min a run."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 52025e37-e99f-41af-81f6-04ea3d9309c8
  modified: 2026-09-29T20:14:13.752Z
---

The fastest honest GEMM screen in the repo (KERNELS.md G1/G2, 2026-09-29): compile the arm with glslc to the scratchpad, then from `h3/dit`:

```
H3_SHAPES=480 H3_PROFILE=1 H3_BANK=q8 H3_GEMM_SPV=$S/arm.spv [H3_GEMM_WAVE=32] \
  [H3_GEMM_KRANGE_SPV=$S/arm_krange.spv] H3_GEMM_REF=$S/ref480.bits \
  ./dit.test -test.run TestGPUShapes -test.v -test.timeout 20m
```

with a 100 ms sampler on `/sys/class/hwmon/hwmon2/{freq1_input,power1_average}` running beside it (mode/percentiles over samples ≥125 W = the forward). ~2.5 min a run (42 GB staging via bank-cache, two 480p forwards). ### 2.10 Every VALU instruction costs the matrix pipe a clock: the LDS-staged GEMM's second K tile as a loop — **done** ✅ (2026-09-29)

**Question** (KERNELS.md G-o8, after §2.9): the shipped LDS-staged wave32
GEMM (`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32`) runs at 80% of the ceiling at its
clock, and with the staging loads all L0 hits at 82%, so the ~18 points
left are on the LDS side of the kernel: 64 `ds_load_b64`, 6 stores, a
barrier and a `lgkmcnt` ladder a slab. Which of those is it?

**Answer: mostly none of them.** The largest single cost was ~40
`v_swap_b32`/`v_mov_b32` a K tile that the register allocator emits to
assemble the slab's *second* tile's fragments, because the scheduler had
hoisted the next slab's six staging loads above this slab's MMAs and the
second tile's `ds_load`s then landed in whatever pairs were free. On this
part **a VALU instruction costs the matrix pipe about one clock** (the
WMMA runs on the SIMD's VALU; there is no separate tensor unit to
overlap with), so those moves were ~7% of the pipe. Keeping the slab's
two K tiles as a loop the compiler may not unroll (`KT_LOOP`), with the
staging views declared writable so NIR does not sink the staging loads to
their use (`STAGE_RW`), takes the moves out: **same MMAs in the same
order, bit-identical**, H3's projections **40.4 → 43.5 TFLOP/s**, the
split down projection 40.3 → 42.2, a 480p forward **27.30 → 26.71 s**,
**80 → 85% per clock**. Shipped as the same build name, so all nine
hosts of the kernel (§2.9's G8 table) get it with no host change.

**The instrument: a probe that adds the kernel's parts back one at a
time.** `shaders/wmma_issue_probe.comp` is the register-only WMMA loop of
`alu_peak.comp` in the GEMM's own geometry (eight wave32 waves of 4×4
tiles, 55 KB of LDS planes at pitch 36), run through `cmd/bench peak` by
the new `PEAK_SPV` hook (`bench/ops_peak.go`), against the same 480
FLOP/clk/CU:

| added to the register-only loop | FLOP/clk/CU | of 480 |
|---|---|---|
| nothing (`wmma_issue_reg`) | 480–491 | 100% |
| 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 independent fp32 FMAs a lane per MMA | 449 / 422 / 382 / 318 | 93.5 / 88 / 80 / 66% |
| a workgroup barrier every 16 MMAs | 480 | 100% |
| the A fragments re-read from LDS each tile (4 a 16 MMAs) | 475 | 99% |
| A and B re-read from LDS (the GEMM's 8 a 16 MMAs, 32 `ds_load_b64`) | 467 | 97% |
| the LDS reads **and** the barrier | 438 | 91% |
| the reads as 16-lane exchanges (`XCHG`: half the LDS bytes, +12 VALU a fragment) | 397 | 83% |
| the exchange and the barrier | 384 | 80% |

FMAs per MMA cost 12%, which is 4 clocks of a 34-clock wave32 MMA, and it
stays linear to 8 a MMA (dual-issue softens 16). So the 16-MMA tile's
budget for everything that is not an MMA is a few instructions, and the
shipped kernel was spending ~50. **The LDS bandwidth is not the limit**:
the GEMM's own read pattern costs 3% (G-o8's "LDS rate for replicated
reads" candidate is dead), and a barrier alone costs nothing. **The two

exchange is 4 permutes and 8 selects a fragment (ACO lowers

python3 - <<'EOF'
import re
p='shaders/dit_gemm.comp'
s=open(p).read()
old="""#ifndef LDS_HALF_READS
#define LDS_HALF_READS 0
#endif
"""
new="""#ifndef LDS_HALF_READS
#define LDS_HALF_READS 0
#endif
// STORE_TILES (KERNELS.md G3, H4): a pricing knob, never shipped, wrong by
// construction. Only the first STORE_TILES of a wave's WM*WN accumulator
// tiles are stored; the rest are stored under a condition that is never
// true at run time (pc.gemmK == 0) and that the compiler cannot decide, so
// every MMA stays and only the epilogue's stores go. At 0 the K loop runs
// alone, and the difference from the shipped build is the epilogue's price.
#ifndef STORE_TILES
#define STORE_TILES (WM * WN)
#endif
"""
assert old in s
s=s.replace(old,new,1)
old2="""    [[unroll]] for (uint i = 0u; i < WM; i++) {
        [[unroll]] for (uint j = 0u; j < WN; j++) {
#if C_PACK
"""
new2="""    [[unroll]] for (uint i = 0u; i < WM; i++) {
        [[unroll]] for (uint j = 0u; j < WN; j++) {
            if (i * WN + j >= uint(STORE_TILES) && pc.gemmK != 0u) { continue; }
#if C_PACK
"""
assert old2 in s
s=s.replace(old2,new2,1)

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

### 2.13 The Q4_K nibble as an f16 denormal: the slab unpack's VALU 331 → 259 a step, bit-identical, `moe.up` 1.02x — and the move storm and the A prefetch priced as dead — **done** ✅ (2026-09-30)

69:| [§2.12](2.12-moe-short-tiles.md) | The grouped MoE GEMM's short last tile: the alignment one fragment, the loop one of WM copies | **`moe.down` 1.23x (1.28x on the served IQ4_NL) and `moe.up` 1.11x at 2048 tokens, bit-identical; prefill 1 417 → 1 514 tok/s at 2048 (1.07x), 1 500 → 1 549 at 4096.** The padding factor 1.90x → 1.19x (the up m4 build executes as 1.41x: any third copy of its loop spills, so it keeps the 2- and 4-tile ones); a control with the alignment forced back to 64 prices the four-copy build at −9%; the m2/m4 boundary moves from 1024 tokens to 256. The short tiles are bound by the slab unpack, ~300 VALU a lane a step at a matrix clock each |
70:| [§2.13](2.13-moe-nibble-denormal.md) | The Q4_K nibble as an f16 denormal: the MoE up GEMM's unpack VALU 331 → 259 a step | **Bit-identical, `moe.up` 1.02x at 512–4096 tokens; whole-model prefill 1 513 → 1 522 tok/s at 2048 (1.006x), 1 548 → 1 555 at 4096, 1 484 → 1 489 at 8192, same-hour A/B twice.** The compiler already fuses the affine and the half conversion into `v_fma_mix`; a halfword holding one nibble *is* the half `nib × 2^-24`, so the extract-and-convert pair goes and the scale carries the power of two. The count predicts 3–5% and buys 2%: the VALU was only partly on the critical path. The m4 build's 71 allocator moves a step are register pressure (the m2 carries four); the K tiles as a loop adds moves, and fetching A at the top of the step removes them for −12%. There is no 5% left in the unpack |
155:| [L6b](l6b-graph.md) | **The model runs end to end: llama.cpp's own token, and 1.82x its prefill.** The five blocks in `llama_model_qwen4exp::graph::graph`'s order plus the two tensors no block owned — the embedding gather and the 675 MB lm head — with **nothing changed in any shader**. On a seven-token prompt the argmax is the reference's (**561**) out of a top ten that is the reference's ten tokens, `result_norm` is **0.519% of scale** and `result_output` **1.983%**. That deep a disagreement is either accumulation or a bug and one number cannot tell them apart, so a second oracle pass filtered to `l_last` every eight layers prices the drift at each depth: **0.034 / 0.055 / 0.103 / 0.154 / 0.330 / 0.881% at 8 through 48 layers**, a clean geometric **x1.085 a layer** with no step at any block — which is what fp16 operands against the reference's int8 dot products (L2b-2) and fp16 accumulators (L4a-5) compound to over 48 residual additions. Three structural facts the reference settles: **there is no output norm** (the final hyper-connection mixer is it, so the head is the vertical's only bare matmul), **the final mixer and the head run on one row** because `inp_out_ids` drops the rest, and **the wide residual never leaves the mixer's arena** because the combine updates it in place — so what crosses a block boundary is 2560 wide, not 10240. **Then the finding that was worth 5.0x, and it was a memory type.** The first working graph was 280.3 tok/s, 0.72x llama.cpp, with 45.5% of its wall clock in host plumbing that moves only 5.24 MB a hop — because the type `NewBuffer` prefers here is write-combined and **the host reads it at 0.18 GB/s**, where a HOST_CACHED type reads the same buffer at **25.06 and writes it 1.4x faster too**: 139x, and DEVICE_LOCAL is one of the slow ones. This is the other half of **L0b**, which measured the same table from the device at 236.0-237.4 GB/s across all of it — so the choice is free on the GPU and decisive on the host, and the control says so: the MoE block runs its layer in **10834.5 us on cached arenas against 10850.2 on write-combined ones, 0.14%**, kept as `LLM_ARENA_UNCACHED=1` rather than as a note. The second half of the plumbing was the f32→fp16 narrowing — 126 million conversions a graph on one core — parallelised over rows for 832 ms → 264. The ladder is **177.3 / 403.7 / 553.9 / 713.9 tok/s at 128 / 512 / 1024 / 2048**, and it **inverts against the reference's**, which peaks at 512 and loses 14% by 2048 on L2a-4's MALL cliff: against llama.cpp *at 2048* the graph is **2.12x**. What is left is the glue at 22.7% — worth the **931.6 tok/s** the blocks alone already do, which [L6c](l6c-moves.md) then collected |
276:| M11 | Performance: the profile's winners; sparse attention if MiniMax publishes it | **M11a done 2026-09-26**: int8 banks for the text encoder and the transformer (`qwen.BankQ8`, served default): 50 → 26.9 GB and 42 → 22.9 GB staged, measured request peak 57 → 32.6 GB at 480p, no speed cost, every teacher-forced step inside the released bf16 pipeline's error. **M11b done 2026-09-29**: the int8 banks and AdaLN tables cached beside the checkpoint (`qwen.Q8Cache`, 47 GB of disk), staging ~94 s → ~12 s of a request, output byte-identical. **M11c done 2026-09-29**: the attention transposed (`h3_attn_t.comp`), so P reaches the matrix cores without LDS: 1.55–1.61x on the kernel, a forward 35.6 → 30.6 s at 480p and 144 → 111 s at 768p, gated teacher-forced. **M11d**: the down projection in two K passes, bit-identical, 1.02x a 480p forward; its swizzle band and row pad screened and already optimal. **M11e**: the video VAE's attention on M11c's transposed kernel at head 64, 1.44x on the kernel, a 480p decode 38.4 → 37.1 s, PSNR against the oracle unchanged at 81.7 dB. **M11f**: the audio decode on the device, priced and not built: the CPU decode already hides under the video decode, and costs a request only the 2.4 s of device time its memory traffic takes from that decode. **M11h** (2026-09-29): the headroom assessed; a 480p forward runs at 33.5 TFLOP/s, 80% of this machine's best kernel, so exact work has ≤ 1.25x left; the row chunk at 4096 is 1.04x measured, not shipped; the multiples are lossy (step caching, block-sparse attention, a 4-step LoRA) and the user's call. **KERNELS.md G2** (2026-09-29): the big GEMM is `dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32` (K slabs staged through LDS at wave32, research §2.9), bit-identical: projections 37 → 41 TFLOP/s, the split down projection 29 → 41, **a 480p forward 29.9 → 27.1 s**; the video VAE on the same build (G8), PSNR unchanged, **a 480p decode 37.1 → 35.5 s**. **KERNELS.md G-o8** (2026-09-29, research §2.10): the same build with its K tiles kept as a loop (the register allocator's ~40 moves a tile were costing the matrix pipe a clock each), bit-identical again: projections 40.4 → 43.5 TFLOP/s, **a 480p forward 27.3 → 26.7 s**. **KERNELS.md G4** (2026-09-30, research §3.8): the transposed attention priced honestly — the softmax 6–7 points, the K/V loads 11–12, the floor 81% per clock — and five exact arms all within ±2% of the shipped build, so nothing changes for H3; the one lever left is the K/V block staged through LDS (G4b, ≤ 2% of a forward) |

### 2.14 The GEMM's epilogue: the fp32 store costs the pipe nothing, the sawtooth is ≤ 5%, and the two passes that read the fp32 C fused into it — **done** ✅ (2026-09-30)

**Question** (KERNELS.md G3, hypotheses H4 and H5 of the reopened
vertical): the shipped GEMM (`dit_gemm_wg128x256_lds_w32`, §2.9/§2.10)
ends with 16 fp32 accumulator tiles a wave stored row-major — 128
`buffer_store_b32` a lane, two 64 B segments each — and H4 priced that
at up to 9% "if nothing overlaps it". H5 asked what the grid's last
round costs as M varies. And KERNELS.md's table asked for `C_F16` and the
fragment-tile C "where the consumer allows".

**Answers.** (1) **The store costs the matrix pipe under a point.** A
live control that keeps every MMA and skips the stores at run time
(`STORE_TILES`, below) runs the same per-clock rate as the shipped build:
the 9% it reads in TFLOP/s is *all clock*, because a forward whose every
downstream kernel runs on zeros draws 130 W instead of 154 and clocks
2900 instead of 2671. (2) **The sawtooth is ≤ 5%** on the q projection,
≤ 2% on gate and ≤ 3% on down past ~1300 rows, and the served 480p chunks
sit near its top; below ~600 rows the grid's ramp dominates, which is
G8's "the build loses below ~1000 rows". (3) What the fp32 C costs is
**what the consumers do with it afterwards**: on the H3 profile the
SwiGLU pass (2.1% of a forward, reading both fp32 halves) and the v
pack (0.9%, only re-laying out the v projection's C as fragment tiles).
Both are epilogues of the GEMM now, bit-identical to the passes they
replace: PLACEHOLDER_RESULT.

#### H4: the store priced with a live control

`-DSTORE_TILES=n` on `dit_gemm.comp` (a pricing knob, never shipped, wrong
by construction): the first n of a wave's 16 accumulator tiles are stored,
the rest under a condition the compiler cannot decide and that is never
true at run time (`pc.gemmK == 0`), so every MMA stays — the ISA holds 48
`v_wmma` and the same K loop as the shipped build — and one uniform
branch skips the stores. `STORE_TILES=8` leaves half the C stale, which is
*real-looking* data from the chunk before (the arenas hold it), so the
forward's power stays near the cap; `STORE_TILES=0` and `1` leave every
downstream kernel on zeros and the package 24 W under it.

H3 480p (`H3_SHAPES=480 H3_PROFILE=1 H3_BANK=q8`, 15 936 rows in chunks
of 8192; the sampler's median clock and package power over the forward;
per clock = FLOP/clk/CU against 480 at that clock):

| build | qkv | gate / up | o | down | forward | sclk | W | per clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| shipped, run 1 (bit-identical, `H3_GEMM_REF` written) | 43.3 | 43.2 / 43.0 | 42.3 | 42.2 | 26.22 s | 2671 | 154 | 405, **84.4%** |
| shipped, run 2 (bit-identical) | 43.7 | 43.2 / 43.1 | 42.1 | 42.2 | 26.33 | 2672 | 154 | 409, 85.2% |
| `STORE_TILES=8`: half the stores | 44.4 | 44.2 / 44.5 | 43.7 | 44.6 | 25.62 | 2746 | 152 | 404, 84.2% |
| `STORE_TILES=1`: one tile of 16 | 46.3 | 46.3 / 46.3 | 46.2 | 45.2 | 24.40 | 2886 | 143 | 401, 83.6% |
| `STORE_TILES=0`: no store | **47.1** | 47.1 / 47.1 | 46.4 | 45.3 | 24.25 | **2900** | **130** | 406, 84.6% |

The rate climbs 9% as the stores go and the per-clock number does not
move (404–409 at every arm, ±0.6%): the store overlaps the other resident
workgroup's K loop entirely, as G1's "flat from 1 to 3+ workgroups a CU"
predicted it would. H4 is dead on the pipe. What the table also says is
where the store *does* cost: the forward at the cap runs 2671 MHz and the
one that writes nothing 2900, and §0.7's rule is that at the cap a joule
is a clock — so the fp32 C is paid for in the energy of writing it and of
reading it back, not in issue slots, and the way to get it back is fewer
bytes through DRAM, which is the fusion below.

`TestGPUGEMMSawtooth` (`H3_SAWTOOTH=480x864`): one real forward fills the

at every row count from 128 to 8192 in steps of 128 (the median of 7),
on the shipped build, at 2678 MHz / 155 W. Rounds = workgroups / 40 (two
128×256 workgroups a WGP by their 55 KB of LDS):

| rows | q (N 7168, K 5376): grid, TFLOP/s | gate (N 14336): grid, TFLOP/s | down (N 5376, K 14336, 2 K pieces): grid, TFLOP/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 28, 17.5 | 56, 18.0 | 21, 15.3 |
| 256 | 56, 25.1 | 112, 28.6 | 42, 19.8 |
| 512 | 112, 37.5 | 224, 37.5 | 84, 29.1 |
| 640 | 140, 39.7 | 280, 44.0 | 105, 39.0 |
| 1024 | 224, 40.2 | 448, 39.8 | 168, 35.9 |
| 1280 | 280, 42.6 | 560, 43.2 | 210, 39.1 |
| 2048 | 448, 41.9 | 896, 42.7 | 336, 40.4 |
| 3456 / 3584 / 3712 / 3840 | 43.8 / 43.9 / **40.8** / **44.5** | 43.5 / 42.8 / 42.7 / 44.2 | 40.1 / 42.2 / 40.6 / 42.6 |
| 4096 | 896, 42.6 | 1792, 43.7 | 672, 41.0 |
| 4736 / 4864 / 4992 | **40.0** / 40.2 / 41.0 | 43.7 / 42.5 / 42.4 | 41.2 / 42.7 / 41.4 |
| 6144 | 1344, 43.5 | 2688, 43.6 | 1008, 41.5 |
| 7808 (the second served chunk) | 1708, 43.5 | 3416, 43.9 | 1281, 41.0 |
| 8192 (the first) | 1792, 43.9 | 3584, 43.5 | 1344, 42.6 |

The plateau is reached by ~640 rows on gate (56 column blocks a row
block, 1.4 rounds a step: the last round is never far from full) and by
~1300 on q and down; above it the q rate swings 40.0–44.5 with the
fractional round (a step of 0.7 round: low just past an integer, high
just under one), gate 42.4–44.5, down 40.1–43.0. The served shape's two
chunks (64 and 61 row blocks) land at 43.5–43.9 on q and gate and 41.0–42.6
on down, at the top of each band, which is why the base profile above reads
43.3 / 43.2 / 42.2. Below ~600 rows the ramp and drain of a grid under two
rounds cost 2x, which is what G8 measured as the build losing to the
wave64 one at Kev's 494 rows and `ace/dit`'s short inputs. Nothing to
fix for H3; a host with a free choice of chunk could pick one whose
fractional round lands high on every projection, worth ≤ 2% of the GEMMs.

#### The fusions

---
name: control-arms-move-the-clock
description: A wrong-by-construction GEMM arm (stores skipped) reads +9% TFLOP/s that is all clock, because every downstream kernel then runs on zeros at 130 W instead of 154; price arms per clock, and prefer controls that leave real-looking data.
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

In the H3 screen a `STORE_TILES=0` GEMM arm (every MMA kept, no C store) read 47.1 TFLOP/s against the shipped 43.3, and the whole 9% was the clock: 2900 MHz at 130 W against 2671 at the 154 W cap, because the forward's other kernels ran on the zeros the GEMM never wrote. Per clock both were 405 FLOP/clk/CU. A `STORE_TILES=8` arm leaves half the C *stale from the previous chunk*, real-looking data, and ran at 2746 MHz / 152 W — the honest control (KERNELS.md G3, research §2.14, 2026-09-30).

**Why:** the package is power-capped, so any arm that changes what the rest of the graph computes changes the clock, and TFLOP/s then measures energy elsewhere, not the kernel.

**How to apply:** every arm needs the sampler beside it and is compared per clock; when an arm must be wrong by construction, make its output stale rather than zero. Related: [[a-benchmark-that-gets-faster]], [[valu-costs-matrix-clocks]].
EOF

**Why:** the package is power-capped, so any arm that changes what the rest of the graph computes changes the clock, and TFLOP/s then measures energy elsewhere, not the kernel.

**How to apply:** every arm needs the sampler beside it and is compared per clock; when an arm must be wrong by construction, make its output stale rather than zero. Related: [[a-benchmark-that-gets-faster]], [[valu-costs-matrix-clocks]].

**What the next item was.** KERNELS.md's handoff left G3 (the GEMM epilogue and grid tail) and G6 open; I took G3, since it is next in the stage table and its two hypotheses had never been measured.

- The v projection is stored straight into the attention's fragment tiles (`C_PACK`, its guard lifted; a new `zero_f16.comp` zeroes the A operand's pad rows first so the pad keys stay +0). The `pack v` dispatch is gone.
- gate and up run as one GEMM over a host-interleaved weight (`projGateUp`, 64-row groups) whose epilogue is the SwiGLU (`C_SWIGLU`). The `swiglu` dispatch and both fp32 halves are gone.
